title: Land Flipping — Operator Companion Workbook
subtitle: 6 Printable Operator Worksheets for Vacant-Land Selection, GIS Underwriting, Parcel Economics, Title-Insured Closings, Minor Subdivisions, and Small-Team Portfolio Control

worksheets.title: Parcel Opportunity Underwriting and Counterparty Qualification
worksheets.purpose: Translate a vacant-land lead into a documented acquisition thesis before committing earnest money. Establish the intended buyer, supportable resale price, usable acreage, recorded access, seller authority, and evidence requirements that distinguish a marketable parcel from a cheap but unsellable liability.
instructions: Choose one county, one parcel category, and one buyer profile before importing owner records. Describe the exit as a specific permitted use, then identify the evidence needed to support that use without relying on listing language.

Create a parcel evidence folder containing assessor records, recorded instruments, zoning sources, comparable deeds, and dated GIS exports. Record each source date and custodian so another operator can reproduce the underwriting without repeating every search.

Separate preliminary screening from acquisition clearance. A mapped road, utility line, or favorable zoning color supports further investigation only; obtain the recorded rights, provider response, and local interpretation required for the proposed exit.

Contact the seller through an approved channel and verify their relationship to the vesting owner before discussing binding terms. Route estates, trusts, entity transfers, and disputed ownership to the settlement team for authority review.

Calculate a maximum acquisition price using supported proceeds and the complete cost stack. Record the exact evidence that would change the decision, and reject opportunities whose economics depend on unapproved subdivision or speculative utility extensions.

fields.name: Target parcel and buyer thesis
fields.prompt: Define the geography, parcel size, current permitted use, buyer segment, and intended disposition. Explain why this segment offers repeatable demand rather than merely a low asking price or attractive aerial photograph.
fields.example: Target existing residential lots of 0.25–0.75 acres within a twenty-minute drive of an established employment center. The buyer is a local builder purchasing one buildable lot. Underwrite an $85,000 resale only when recent closed lots support similar frontage, utilities, and permitted housing density.

fields.name: Parcel identity and source chain
fields.prompt: Record the assessor parcel identifier, vesting deed reference, legal description source, acreage discrepancies, and evidence timestamps. Explain how the settlement agent will resolve differences between tax mapping and the conveyed property.
fields.example: Working parcel LF-018-001 has assessor acreage of 0.52 and deed acreage of 0.49. The acquisition file retains the recorded deed, assessor export, and survey request. Pricing uses the smaller acreage until the surveyor and title examiner reconcile boundaries and the conveyance description.

fields.name: Seller identity and signing authority
fields.prompt: Identify the vesting owner, proposed signer, ownership form, and authority documents required for closing. Describe the independent verification method and any ownership dispute that would stop negotiations or release of funds.
fields.example: The vesting owner is an LLC, while the inquiry came from a member using a personal email address. Escrow requests formation records, operating authority, and signer identification through its secure portal. No deposit leaves escrow until the settlement team accepts the signing authority.

fields.name: Recorded access and physical access
fields.prompt: Distinguish public frontage, recorded easement rights, physical passability, and maintenance obligations. Identify the instruments and professional review needed to demonstrate access suitable for the proposed buyer's use and likely construction traffic.
fields.example: An aerial image shows a gravel lane, but the deed does not establish access rights. Request the recorded easement, benefited parcel description, width, maintenance terms, and title treatment. Reject the acquisition if residential and construction access cannot be established before the inspection deadline.

fields.name: Zoning and minor-subdivision feasibility
fields.prompt: Record current zoning, minimum lot dimensions, setbacks, frontage standards, and the local subdivision process. Separate an existing-parcel resale from a proposed split, including required approvals, infrastructure conditions, fees, and processing dependencies.
fields.example: The parent tract contains 1.20 acres, but a proposed three-lot split requires minimum frontage that one child lot lacks. Underwrite the existing parcel only. A subdivision case must separately price surveying, application fees, improvement conditions, recording, and the county's written processing sequence.

fields.name: Utilities and buildable-envelope evidence
fields.prompt: Document water, wastewater, power, drainage, and usable building area using provider and professional evidence. Distinguish nearby infrastructure from an enforceable connection opportunity with known capacity, extension scope, and buyer responsibilities.
fields.example: Water is visible across the street, but the provider quotes a $12,000 connection and road-crossing package. The resale comparison assumes connected lots, so either deduct that burden from supported value or obtain comparable unconnected sales. A nearby main does not establish available capacity.

fields.name: Environmental and terrain screening
fields.prompt: List flood, wetland, slope, dumping, historic-use, and habitat indicators, together with their source dates. Identify which conditions require field investigation and how unresolved constraints affect usable acreage, pricing, and acquisition timing.
fields.example: County terrain data suggests a steep rear section, and a federal wetland inventory shows a mapped feature nearby. Exclude the rear section from the preliminary building envelope. Commission appropriate field review before pricing a homesite that depends on grading or filling that area.

fields.name: Closed-sale comparison and liquidity
fields.prompt: Select verified closed sales with comparable rights, utilities, size, and permitted use. Record sale dates, concessions, market exposure, and adjustments, explaining why active asking prices do not establish executable resale proceeds.
fields.example: Three verified comparable lots closed at $82,000, $86,000, and $89,000 after 74, 103, and 118 market days. The highest sale included a paid connection fee. Support an $85,000 subject resale only after adjusting that benefit and confirming similar recorded access and usable frontage.

fields.name: Counterparty and settlement qualification
fields.prompt: Qualify the listing broker, settlement provider, survey resource, and likely buyer for land-specific execution. Record capacity, service scope, verification procedures, fee evidence, and the failure that would trigger replacement of each provider.
fields.example: The broker supplies five recent vacant-lot closings and accepts a negotiated $3,375 disposition fee. Escrow confirms its title-underwriting relationship and independent wire-verification procedure. The diligence contractor provides survey coordination and identifies when a separately licensed environmental or engineering specialist must be engaged.

fields.name: Acquisition decision and maximum bid
fields.prompt: State the supported resale amount, complete nonpurchase cost stack, required owner profit, and resulting maximum bid. Name unresolved evidence and specify whether the decision is rejection, conditional pursuit, or documented acquisition readiness.
fields.example: At $85,000 proceeds, subtract $15,725 target profit, $2,200 buy-side closing, $1,800 diligence, $1,500 expected cure work, $2,400 carrying, $3,375 selling, and $10,000 overhead allocation. Maximum acquisition price is $48,000. Pursue conditionally, with recorded access and utility evidence still required before closing.

worksheets.completion_gate: The owner signs a dated investment memo identifying the parcel, verified seller authority, supported buyer use, three reviewed comparables, maximum bid, and every unresolved acquisition condition. No unresolved access or buildability assumption is described as established.

worksheets.title: Unit Economics, Defect Reserve, and Working-Capital Float
worksheets.purpose: Reconcile parcel-level decisions to the canonical annual scorecard while keeping purchase capital, operating expenses, reserves, and sale proceeds distinct. Model the cash trapped in unsold inventory, the effect of slower exits, and the exact bid reductions needed when defects or selling costs increase.
instructions: Use gross parcel sale proceeds as the revenue basis for owned-land trading. Include acquisition costs in the net-margin calculation, exclude borrowed principal from revenue, and keep seller deposits and owner contributions outside earned operating income.

Build each parcel budget from purchase price through disposition, then allocate annual overhead consistently. Mark forecasts as forecasts and replace them with incurred costs at close; an unspent cash reserve does not become an expense automatically.

Reconcile Conservative, Base, and Scaled annual totals before using a parcel calculator. Changes to resale prices, volume, staffing, or cost assumptions belong in a separately labeled sensitivity case rather than an altered canonical scorecard.

Construct a monthly cash schedule showing deposits, acquisitions, diligence, cure payments, carrying costs, and closing receipts. Stress the acquisition cadence against delayed dispositions, because an attractive annual margin can still exhaust available cash.

Set a cash floor and acquisition-pause trigger before making offers. Tie contingency releases to documented risk retirement, and distinguish parcel-level carrying costs from enterprise overhead so the same invoice is never deducted twice.

fields.name: Canonical scenario reconciliation
fields.prompt: Enter the three required annual revenue, margin, owner-profit, and staffing combinations. Explain the revenue basis and identify which scenario is the operating plan without presenting the other scenarios as interchangeable forecasts.
fields.example: Conservative: $200,000 revenue × 12% = $24,000 owner profit, with 1 FT + 3 C. Base: $850,000 × 18.5% = $157,250, with 1 FT + 3 C. Scaled: $1,500,000 × 25% = $375,000, with 2 FT + 4 C. Revenue means gross owned-parcel sale proceeds.

fields.name: Base parcel cost stack
fields.prompt: List acquisition, purchase closing, diligence, expected defect work, carrying, disposition, and allocated overhead separately. Show the total cost and owner contribution for one representative parcel using the Base scenario assumptions.
fields.example: One $85,000 sale carries $48,000 acquisition, $2,200 purchase closing, $1,800 diligence, $1,500 expected cure work, $2,400 carrying, $3,375 disposition, and $10,000 overhead. Total cost is $69,275; owner profit is $15,725. Ten identical completed sales reconcile exactly to the Base annual scorecard.

fields.name: Annual volume and expense bridge
fields.prompt: Translate annual proceeds into an illustrative count of completed sales and average selling price. Reconcile total expenses and enterprise overhead without implying that these illustrative parcel counts are additional canonical operating requirements.
fields.example: Illustratively, Conservative sells four parcels at $50,000, with $176,000 total costs including $36,000 overhead. Base sells ten at $85,000, with $692,750 costs including $100,000 overhead. Scaled sells fifteen at $100,000, with $1,125,000 costs including $180,000 overhead. Each produces the required scenario profit.

fields.name: Scrub failures and defect reserve
fields.prompt: Estimate rejected-lead diligence and acquired-parcel cure exposure using explicit probabilities or observed cohorts. Separate cash earmarks from recognized expenses, and state how actual spending changes the forecast and final parcel margin.
fields.example: Budget $18,000 annual diligence, including abandoned-lead research, and allocate it across ten completed sales. Separately forecast $15,000 of incurred cure work, or $1,500 per sale. If only $9,000 is incurred, owner profit rises by $6,000 with other costs unchanged; unused earmarks are not expenses.

fields.name: Inventory float and startup funding
fields.prompt: Calculate cash committed before disposition across concurrent parcel slots. Add overhead runway and a separate liquidity buffer, identify the funding source, and compare the result with the stated startup capital range.
fields.example: Each slot commits $55,900 before selling fees: purchase, buy-side closing, diligence, cure work, and carrying. Three slots require $167,700. Add $50,000 for six months of Base overhead and $20,000 liquidity buffer: $237,700 startup funding, within the $50,000–$400,000 range. Selling fees are deducted at disposition.

fields.name: Cash conversion and holding delay
fields.prompt: Specify acquisition-to-cash timing, monthly parcel carrying costs, and the effect of slower closings. Distinguish a cost sensitivity from an annual volume shortfall, and avoid assuming inventory proceeds arrive merely because listings are active.
fields.example: The Base parcel carries for four months at $600 monthly, totaling $2,400. A three-month delay adds $1,800 and reduces parcel profit to $13,925. Across ten unchanged sales, profit becomes $139,250; if fewer sales close that year, rebuild annual revenue and inventory separately.

fields.name: Resale haircut and bid sensitivity
fields.prompt: Stress supported proceeds downward while holding clearly identified costs constant. Calculate revised dollar profit, revised margin, and the acquisition-price adjustment required to preserve the original dollar contribution under that sensitivity.
fields.example: A 10% resale haircut reduces $85,000 to $76,500. With the original $69,275 cost stack unchanged, profit is $7,225 and margin is approximately 9.44%. Preserving $15,725 dollar profit requires reducing acquisition from $48,000 to $39,500, assuming every other cost remains fixed.

fields.name: Funding terms and debt separation
fields.prompt: Document equity, loan proceeds, repayment dates, interest, origination charges, and collateral restrictions. Show how financing costs enter parcel economics while principal movements remain separate from sale revenue and operating profit.
fields.example: A proposed $40,000 loan at 12% simple annual interest for six months adds $2,400 interest plus an $800 origination charge. Unless already budgeted, the $3,200 reduces Base parcel profit to $12,525. The $40,000 advance and principal repayment are funding movements, not revenue or duplicate acquisition expense.

fields.name: Operating runway and acquisition pause
fields.prompt: Set monthly enterprise spending, minimum unrestricted cash, and a pause rule based on expected obligations. Explain how the team distinguishes available cash from escrowed deposits, restricted reserves, and optimistic projected sales.
fields.example: Base annual overhead of $100,000 equals about $8,333.33 monthly, with a final-month rounding adjustment. Maintain $20,000 unrestricted liquidity beyond committed parcel spending. Pause new deposits when a thirteen-week cash forecast falls below that floor, even if listed inventory appears to contain substantial paper profit.

fields.name: Closeout reconciliation and owner distributions
fields.prompt: Describe the parcel closeout process linking settlement statements, invoices, inventory cost release, overhead, and owner withdrawals. Identify the records that prove the annual profit bridge without treating distributions as operating expenses.
fields.example: Ten Base sales produce $850,000 revenue against $480,000 acquisition, $22,000 purchase closing, $18,000 diligence, $15,000 cure work, $24,000 carrying, $33,750 selling, and $100,000 overhead. Expenses total $692,750 and owner profit equals $157,250. Owner draws reduce cash and equity, not this operating expense bridge.

worksheets.completion_gate: Every scenario reconciles to its canonical revenue and owner profit; the Base parcel totals $69,275 cost and $15,725 profit. The owner approves a thirteen-week cash forecast, explicit reserve treatment, and a funded acquisition-pause threshold before issuing offers.

worksheets.title: Execution Ledger and Parcel Technical QA Pre-Flight
worksheets.purpose: Control the complete parcel lifecycle from accepted offer through recorded disposition. Use evidence-linked status changes, reproducible GIS checks, title exception review, settlement controls, and cost reconciliation to prevent mismatched parcels, missed deadlines, unsupported marketing claims, and funds released against incomplete closing conditions.
instructions: Assign one internal deal identifier and preserve the county parcel identifier separately. Use the internal identifier across contracts, GIS layers, invoices, title files, and listings; never substitute a street address for a verified legal description.

Create a dated execution ledger with one accountable owner for each transition. Link source documents rather than summarizing them from memory, and make inspection expiration, title objections, deposit changes, and closing deadlines visible together.

Run GIS screening in a known coordinate system and record layer dates, limitations, and geometry checks. Escalate apparent boundary, access, or flood conflicts to the relevant professional instead of treating a map overlay as a survey.

Review the title commitment and settlement requirements before the acquisition deadline. Track each exception through acceptance, cure, or rejection, and require documented confirmation when a requested coverage provision cannot actually be issued.

Before disposition, compare every listing claim with the evidence packet and reconcile estimated seller proceeds to the signed settlement statement. Complete the ledger only after recording evidence, funds confirmation, and unresolved post-closing items are captured.

fields.name: Deal identifier and document register
fields.prompt: Define the parcel naming convention, document version rules, and authoritative sources for legal description and ownership. Explain how revised contracts or assessor changes are linked without erasing the evidence supporting earlier decisions.
fields.example: Use LF-018-001 as the permanent deal identifier and store the county parcel number in a separate field. The executed contract is version 03, linked to its signed amendment. The vesting deed supplies the initial legal description; escrow verifies the final conveyance description against its title examination.

fields.name: Contract dates and deposit ledger
fields.prompt: Record acceptance, inspection expiration, title objection, cure, closing, and extension dates with the controlling contract language. Track deposit amount, holder, refund conditions, and the person responsible for timely notices.
fields.example: The contract is accepted June 3, with inspection ending June 24 at the stated local time and closing July 15. A $1,000 deposit is credited toward the $48,000 purchase price. Calendar reminders occur seven and three days before inspection expiration; the owner sends any required notice.

fields.name: GIS geometry and coordinate checks
fields.prompt: Specify the GIS software, source coordinate systems, geometry validation, acreage checks, and overlay tolerances. Explain which discrepancies are screening flags and which require survey evidence before the parcel can advance.
fields.example: QGIS imports county parcel polygons and reprojects them to a suitable local projected coordinate system before measuring area. Check invalid rings, duplicate features, and missing identifiers. A 0.03-acre difference from the deed is logged for survey review, not silently replaced by the GIS measurement.

fields.name: Title commitment and exception disposition
fields.prompt: Record the proposed insured owner, estate, policy amount, requirements, and exceptions. Assign a disposition to each material exception and identify written insurer confirmation needed for access, liens, restrictions, or requested endorsements.
fields.example: The acquisition commitment names the purchasing LLC and a $48,000 proposed policy amount. Escrow requires payoff of a recorded lien. A restrictive covenant remains for use review. Request available access coverage in writing; do not assume a standard policy resolves every physical-access or zoning concern.

fields.name: Survey and field inspection acceptance
fields.prompt: Define the survey scope and field inspection evidence needed for the intended exit. Capture encroachments, monuments, frontage, dumping, fences, and drainage observations, including who determines whether a discovered condition is acceptable.
fields.example: The survey request identifies boundary location, road frontage, visible encroachments, and recorded easements relevant to the purchase. Site photographs show a neighbor's fence inside the apparent boundary. The owner pauses acquisition while the surveyor, title examiner, and transaction counsel evaluate the encroachment and possible cure.

fields.name: Subdivision task sequence and release
fields.prompt: If a split is proposed, map application, conditions, engineering, surveying, recording, and child-parcel creation. Explain what must occur before child lots are marketed or sold, and isolate subdivision economics from the existing-parcel Base example.
fields.example: The proposed two-lot project receives a separate project code and budget. Planning confirmation precedes survey design; conditions are priced before filing. No child lot is advertised as legally created until required mapping and recording steps are complete. The existing-lot Base budget does not fund this entitlement work.

fields.name: Invoice coding and inventory ledger
fields.prompt: Assign parcel costs and enterprise expenses to consistent ledger categories, documenting the accounting treatment approved for the business. Explain allocation of failed-lead costs and prevent invoice duplication between parcel budgets and overhead.
fields.example: The management ledger assigns a $900 survey invoice to LF-018-001 diligence and an $85 CRM subscription to enterprise overhead. Failed-lead research remains visible in the annual diligence pool. The accountant determines capitalization and tax treatment; the management bridge still reconciles all costs to annual owner profit.

fields.name: Wire verification and closing pre-flight
fields.prompt: Specify how settlement instructions, recipient identity, payoff figures, deed execution, and cash requirements are independently verified. Identify the stop condition for changed instructions and the evidence retained after funds are transmitted.
fields.example: Before sending acquisition funds, the owner calls escrow using a previously verified number, confirms account details, and matches the final cash requirement to the statement. A last-minute emailed account change stops transmission. Retain callback notes and bank confirmation without copying full account credentials into the general CRM.

fields.name: Listing evidence and disposition QA
fields.prompt: Compare asking price, parcel dimensions, access, utility, zoning, and subdivision claims with current evidence. Define who approves listing revisions and how the buyer receives relevant documents without exposing unnecessary seller or payment information.
fields.example: The listing states residential zoning and links the dated local source, but does not promise permit issuance. Utility language identifies the provider's written connection estimate. The broker removes an unsupported 'ready to build' claim and supplies buyers a redacted survey, title summary, and documented access description.

fields.name: Post-closing receipt and exception ledger
fields.prompt: Describe how recorded instruments, issued title coverage, net proceeds, tax reporting, and remaining obligations are confirmed after closing. Set an aging threshold for missing documents and assign responsibility for clearing each item.
fields.example: The $85,000 sale is marked closed only after escrow confirms recording and the bank confirms collected proceeds. The issued policy and final statement are requested within the agreed service period. Missing documents remain open in a weekly exception queue, with escrow follow-up assigned to the owner.

worksheets.completion_gate: A second reviewer or designated settlement professional checks the legal description, deadline ledger, material title items, and closing figures. Every material exception has evidence of cure, documented acceptance within the investment thesis, or a stop decision.

worksheets.title: Statutory, Licensing, Contract, and Outreach Audit
worksheets.purpose: Translate applicable land-use, brokerage, environmental, settlement, and outreach rules into documented operating requirements. Identify the actual jurisdiction and transaction structure before selecting forms or marketing language, with special attention to subdivision creation, seller authority, title representations, tax withholding, and permission-sensitive outreach.
instructions: Start with the property's state, county, municipality, and transaction structure. Record the controlling sources and verification date; a rule from a neighboring county or a residential-house form does not automatically fit a vacant-land transaction.

Separate selling property the business owns from representing another owner or marketing contractual rights. Confirm the state-specific licensing and disclosure requirements for each activity before paying transaction-based compensation or publishing the offer.

Have the transaction professional review contract contingencies, title delivery, disclosures, deposit release, and recording requirements against the actual parcel. Convert required actions into named tasks with due dates rather than attaching unused statutory excerpts.

Review environmental and water-related triggers before disturbing soil or assuming development capacity. Screening maps identify questions; appropriate investigations and agency determinations resolve them when the intended use depends on regulated land or water features.

Audit each outreach channel separately for identification, permission, suppression, and record-retention requirements. Store the evidence supporting contact eligibility, and disable automation when eligibility cannot be established or a recipient withdraws permission.

fields.name: Jurisdiction and controlling-source register
fields.prompt: Identify the parcel's governing jurisdictions and official sources for zoning, subdivision, recording, taxation, and broker licensing. Record the effective version and verification date, including any written agency interpretation used in underwriting.
fields.example: For an illustrative California acquisition, retain the county zoning ordinance, subdivision ordinance, recorder checklist, and state licensing source. A planning email dated May 12 explains frontage treatment for this parcel. The register distinguishes that parcel-specific response from the broader ordinance and records who confirmed its continuing applicability.

fields.name: Principal trading versus licensed representation
fields.prompt: Describe whether the business sells owned land, represents another party, or transfers contract rights. Identify the applicable licensing analysis, compensation restrictions, required disclosures, and evidence that marketing accurately reflects the business's role.
fields.example: The LLC purchases and resells its own parcel; it does not accept a neighbor's listing for a success fee. California Business and Professions Code sections 10130, 10131, and 10133 inform the role review. Any proposed representation service is routed to a properly licensed broker before outreach begins.

fields.name: Subdivision mapping and public-report analysis
fields.prompt: Record proposed lot count, contiguous project ownership, local mapping requirements, and state sale requirements. Distinguish map approval from permission to offer lots and identify exemptions only when the actual project satisfies their conditions.
fields.example: For a California three-lot proposal, review Government Code sections 66424 and 66428 plus local parcel-map rules. Separately examine Business and Professions Code sections 11000 and 11010 for the broader project and any public-report requirement. Splitting phases does not by itself establish an exemption.

fields.name: Environmental liability and inquiry timing
fields.prompt: Identify historical-use concerns and the investigation needed before acquisition. If relying on a federal landowner liability protection, document the relevant qualification, inquiry timing, and continuing obligations rather than treating a report as blanket protection.
fields.example: A former equipment yard triggers environmental review before purchase. The specialist evaluates all appropriate inquiries under 40 CFR Part 312 and relevant CERCLA conditions in 42 U.S.C. 9601(40) and 9607(r). Confirm the one-year inquiry window, specified 180-day updates, and continuing obligations for any intended protection.

fields.name: Wetlands, fill, drainage, and site disturbance
fields.prompt: Describe proposed disturbance and possible regulated waters or drainage features. Identify the federal, state, and local determinations or permits needed before grading, filling, clearing, or advertising a development envelope dependent on those activities.
fields.example: A buyer's proposed driveway crosses a wet area. Before pricing the parcel as driveway-ready, investigate Clean Water Act section 404, 33 U.S.C. 1344, and applicable section 401 certification under 33 U.S.C. 1341. Agency jurisdiction, permit needs, and state wetland rules require project-specific review; inventory maps alone do not settle them.

fields.name: Contract protections and factual disclosures
fields.prompt: Specify inspection rights, title objections, access verification, deposit treatment, seller representations, and required property disclosures. Explain how known adverse facts reach the buyer and why a general condition clause does not replace required disclosure.
fields.example: Draft terms allow termination by written notice before inspection expiration if recorded access or the intended use cannot be verified. The seller identifies a known dumping area in a signed attachment. Transaction counsel selects applicable vacant-land disclosures rather than automatically reusing a one-to-four-unit housing disclosure package.

fields.name: Settlement taxes, withholding, and reporting
fields.prompt: Identify seller tax-status documentation, potential withholding, information reporting, transfer taxes, and responsible settlement parties. Distinguish the amount realized from the seller's gain and require written resolution of any claimed withholding exception.
fields.example: A foreign seller's $48,000 sale receives FIRPTA review under 26 U.S.C. 1445. The general 15% calculation is $7,200 of amount realized unless an applicable exception or adjustment is established. Escrow also assigns real-estate reporting under 26 U.S.C. 6045(e); vacant land does not automatically satisfy residence-based exceptions.

fields.name: Email outreach and suppression controls
fields.prompt: Describe the commercial email audience, sender identification, subject-line review, physical address, unsubscribe method, and suppression timing. Identify the party monitoring vendors and explain how suppressed addresses are prevented from reentering later campaigns.
fields.example: Builder outreach uses accurate sender information, a truthful parcel-specific subject, advertising identification where required, a postal address, and an operational unsubscribe link. Under 15 U.S.C. 7704, eligible opt-out requests are honored within ten business days. The CRM checks the suppression list before every send and vendor upload.

fields.name: Telephone, text, and direct-mail eligibility
fields.prompt: Identify calling or texting technology, message purpose, permission evidence, applicable do-not-call restrictions, and state requirements. Separately describe truthful direct-mail practices, and establish an immediate stop when contact eligibility is unresolved.
fields.example: Do not infer texting permission from a public assessor record. Review 47 U.S.C. 227, 47 CFR 64.1200, and applicable state rules for the proposed technology and campaign. Disable automated calls and texts until eligibility is established. Postal offers identify the actual buyer and avoid government-style notices or misleading urgency.

fields.name: Electronic records, privacy, and retention
fields.prompt: Define secure handling of identity records, signatures, contact information, and transaction evidence. Record applicable retention requirements and distinguish electronic contract validity from notarization, delivery, and county recording acceptance for a particular instrument.
fields.example: E-SIGN, 15 U.S.C. 7001, supports qualifying electronic records but does not eliminate every deed execution or recording requirement. Escrow confirms the recorder's accepted process. Identity files remain in restricted storage; the CRM retains only verification status. A written retention schedule incorporates applicable state and transaction requirements.

worksheets.completion_gate: The owner and appropriate transaction specialists resolve every applicable licensing, land-use, environmental, contract, withholding, and outreach question in a source-linked register. Unresolved items remain explicit stop conditions for the affected purchase, listing, site activity, or communication channel.

worksheets.title: Automation Pipeline, Growth Flywheel, and Risk Fallbacks
worksheets.purpose: Automate repeatable parcel screening and comparable-sale tracking without converting imperfect public data into false acquisition certainty. Build a measured sourcing and buyer-development system with source lineage, communication controls, human exception handling, and practical fallbacks when data feeds, provider responses, or market liquidity deteriorate.
instructions: Define the input contract for every data feed, including permitted use, refresh cadence, parcel identifiers, and required fields. Reject malformed records visibly, and preserve source lineage so a scoring decision can be reconstructed after an update.

Automate exclusions and prioritization before attempting automated valuation. Keep legal access, seller authority, environmental interpretation, and buildability decisions under qualified human review; a clean data row is not evidence that those transaction risks are resolved.

Connect outbound work to a narrow buyer thesis and documented contact eligibility. Measure progression from eligible records to responses, qualified conversations, accepted offers, and closed sales rather than celebrating imported records or gross message volume.

Keep comparable-sale monitoring separate from listing-price monitoring. Record verification, concessions, rights, utilities, and market exposure, then flag changes that affect current inventory instead of silently replacing the assumptions used when it was purchased.

For each automation, assign an owner, alert threshold, manual fallback, and restart condition. Test stale data, duplicate events, failed sends, and provider outages before the workflow can change a deal status or initiate external communication.

fields.name: Source inventory and permitted-use contract
fields.prompt: List county GIS, assessor, recorder, listing, and contact sources with access terms, refresh cadence, and required fields. Explain how licensed datasets remain segregated from public records and how expired access stops downstream processing.
fields.example: The county GIS export refreshes monthly and supplies parcel identifiers, geometry, and acreage. Recorder documents support deed verification. Broker-provided sales data stays within its licensed use. Each imported batch records source, retrieval date, terms reference, and checksum; an expired data license suspends that connector rather than reusing restricted exports.

fields.name: Parcel normalization and duplicate prevention
fields.prompt: Define normalization for parcel identifiers, owner names, mailing addresses, geometry, and jurisdiction. Explain how the pipeline handles leading zeros, multi-parcel ownership, changed identifiers, and repeated records without merging distinct properties.
fields.example: Store parcel identifiers as strings so leading zeros survive CSV imports. Use county code plus normalized parcel identifier as the current record key. Link an owner's four parcels without combining their geometry. A parcel renumbering creates a reviewed predecessor link instead of overwriting the historical deal record.

fields.name: Screening rules and exception routing
fields.prompt: Specify reproducible filters for target size, zoning, location, ownership, and apparent constraints. Separate hard exclusions from review flags and identify which evidence allows a reviewer to override an automated result.
fields.example: Screen for 0.25–0.75-acre residential parcels inside the chosen service area. Flag apparent landlocked geometry, steep terrain, and wetland intersections for review. A flag never becomes a confirmed legal conclusion. Overrides require a named reviewer and linked evidence, such as a recorded access easement accepted by the title examiner.

fields.name: Comparable-sale tracking and drift alerts
fields.prompt: Describe the verified-sale data structure, update schedule, adjustment method, and repricing alert. Explain how active listings, stale transactions, unusual concessions, and dissimilar utility conditions are prevented from distorting the underwriting range.
fields.example: A weekly review adds closed sales with deed reference, closing date, utility status, access, and exposure time. An alert fires when three new comparable closings support a range more than 8% below the current $85,000 exit assumption. Active listings remain a separate competition view rather than verified sale evidence.

fields.name: Seller outreach cohort and response ledger
fields.prompt: Define a bounded sourcing cohort, eligible channels, offer logic, response categories, and follow-up limits. Track actual acquisition funnel outcomes and prevent repeat contact after suppression, ownership disputes, or a clear request to stop.
fields.example: The pilot sends 100 individually checked postal offers to owners of screened lots. Log 12 responses, four qualified conversations, two document-ready opportunities, and one conditional offer as observed pilot results only if achieved. Every refusal updates suppression, and the same owner is not approached repeatedly through duplicate parcel records.

fields.name: Builder network and buyer qualification
fields.prompt: Identify buyer segments, acquisition criteria, proof-of-funds handling, viewing process, and repeat-purchase signals. Explain how buyer feedback improves parcel selection without disclosing confidential seller terms or promising an unverified development outcome.
fields.example: Interview ten local builders about frontage, utility cost tolerance, price ceiling, and closing speed. Three prefer serviced lots below $90,000 and request future inventory notices. Obtain appropriate communication permission, record criteria, and verify purchase capacity through the settlement process rather than storing bank statements in an unrestricted marketing folder.

fields.name: Workflow controls and communication eligibility
fields.prompt: Map the transition from screened parcel to reviewed opportunity, authorized offer, and scheduled follow-up. Specify which actions require human authorization and how suppression, channel eligibility, and stale evidence block external messages.
fields.example: Airtable stores review status while a scheduled Python job prepares an internal offer queue. The owner reviews price and recipient before any offer is sent. Suppressed contacts and expired evidence block queue release. No workflow signs contracts, changes escrow instructions, or treats a suggested bid as an accepted commitment.

fields.name: Automation quality test and audit sample
fields.prompt: Define representative test cases, acceptable error thresholds, sampling frequency, and incident ownership. Include duplicates, missing source dates, mismatched jurisdictions, and contradictory access indicators, with evidence showing how failed records are isolated.
fields.example: Test twenty fixtures, including a leading-zero parcel identifier, a county-name collision, duplicate owner records, and a polygon beside an unrecorded road. Any cross-county merge blocks deployment. Review ten newly screened records weekly and retain before-and-after evidence when correcting rules, so earlier acquisition assumptions can be reevaluated.

fields.name: Data outage and provider fallback
fields.prompt: Name the failure signals for source outages, stale exports, missing provider responses, and communication errors. Assign a manual fallback and restart test, ensuring the team does not silently reuse old evidence as current information.
fields.example: If the monthly county feed is more than forty-five days old, pause automated prioritization and verify active deals directly with official records. If the title provider misses a committed response date, escalate and evaluate a qualified replacement. Restart requires a validated fresh batch and review of affected open opportunities.

fields.name: Illiquidity fallback and learning loop
fields.prompt: Set inventory aging thresholds, buyer-feedback reviews, repricing authority, and the conditions for pausing acquisitions. Explain how realized selling results update future screening without disguising a liquidation loss or extending unsupported valuation assumptions.
fields.example: At ninety listing days without a qualified offer, review inquiries, showing feedback, and new closed sales. At 120 days, model a reduced-price cash exit and update the thirteen-week cash forecast. Pause new purchases if liquidity falls below $20,000. Record any loss explicitly and tighten future selection rules using the observed failure.

worksheets.completion_gate: The screening pipeline passes its test set, every outward message has channel eligibility and owner authorization, and stale-source or suppression failures stop affected work. Parcel screening and comparable-sale tracking remain assistive systems, with accountable reviewers for material acquisition conclusions.

worksheets.title: 30-Day Launch Sprint, Pod KPI Scorecard, and Exit Ledger
worksheets.purpose: Launch a focused land-trading operation with measurable evidence production rather than premature revenue promises. Assign small-team responsibilities, sequence thirty days of setup and sourcing, monitor capital and inventory quality, and preserve the records needed to sell individual parcels or transfer an organized operating business.
instructions: Treat the first thirty days as system construction and qualified pipeline development, not a mandatory closing window. The stated time to first deal is three to twelve months, so capital planning must accommodate a prolonged initial acquisition cycle.

Assign the canonical Base pod before setting activity targets: one full-time owner and three contractor roles. Define deliverables, capacity, and escalation paths, and purchase specialist services by scope without hiding their cost or workload.

Schedule market selection, source setup, professional onboarding, pilot outreach, and evidence-backed underwriting in that order. Do not accelerate offers simply to satisfy a launch calendar when access, title, seller authority, or liquidity remains unresolved.

Review leading indicators weekly and realized economics monthly. Keep records screened, conversations, offers, accepted contracts, closed sales, and collected cash separate, with explicit denominators and dates so the scorecard cannot mistake activity for completed revenue.

Maintain an exit ledger from the first purchase, including inventory cost, market evidence, title documents, provider contracts, and open obligations. A possible business transfer requires portable records and defensible earnings, not merely a stack of parcel listings.

fields.name: Strategic position and launch constraints
fields.prompt: Record the candidate's rank, score, capital range, operating expense range, and first-deal timing. Explain how these constraints shape the initial county, parcel category, acquisition cadence, and acceptable dependence on outside expertise.
fields.example: Land Flipping is Candidate #6, pipeline rank #18 of 29, scoring 72/100 as a Disciplined Specialist Play. Startup capital is $50,000–$400,000, monthly operating expense is $3,000–$15,000, and first-deal timing is 3–12 months. Launch in one county with existing lots rather than funding speculative subdivision work.

fields.name: Pod roles and capacity commitments
fields.prompt: Assign the full-time owner and three contractor roles for the Base plan, including deliverables and backup arrangements. Distinguish contractor service costs from permanent staffing and describe the capacity change required for the Scaled plan.
fields.example: Base uses one full-time owner for underwriting and capital decisions, plus three contractor roles: diligence coordination, title and settlement, and disposition brokerage. Specialist engagements are scoped through the relevant role and separately budgeted. Scaled uses 2 FT + 4 C, six people total; additional transaction volume requires demonstrated capacity, not assumed availability.

fields.name: Days 1–7 market and evidence setup
fields.prompt: Specify first-week deliverables for county selection, buyer interviews, source access, record structure, and professional onboarding. Define completion through usable evidence and confirmed service scope rather than meetings booked or software accounts opened.
fields.example: By day seven, select one county, interview five builders, document ten closed-sale candidates, and confirm escrow and diligence service scopes. Create the deal register, evidence folder structure, and thirteen-week cash template. Completion requires source-linked records and written provider responses, not an unreviewed owner list or a generic market presentation.

fields.name: Days 8–14 screening and economics pilot
fields.prompt: Define the second-week screening sample, quality checks, valuation work, and funding review. Explain what constitutes a qualified acquisition candidate and which findings require rejection before any seller receives a binding commitment.
fields.example: Screen 100 parcels and manually audit twenty records. Build complete preliminary economics for five candidates, including access evidence requests and utility assumptions. Verify the $237,700 illustrative three-slot funding plan against actual available funds. Reject apparent bargains whose supported exit cannot cover all costs and the required owner contribution.

fields.name: Days 15–21 controlled sourcing pilot
fields.prompt: Set a bounded outreach pilot, qualification checklist, offer authority, and response review cadence. Distinguish target activities from achieved results and identify what must be documented before a conditional offer is released.
fields.example: Prepare up to 100 reviewed postal contacts and log actual delivery and response outcomes. For each responsive owner, confirm the parcel and relationship to the vesting owner. Release a conditional offer only after owner review of price, inspection rights, deposit exposure, and funding. The sprint target does not require an accepted contract.

fields.name: Days 22–30 review and acquisition readiness
fields.prompt: Describe the final-week review of pilot results, deal files, provider performance, and cash capacity. Define the next thirty-day commitment using evidence, including the acceptable outcome when no parcel satisfies the investment criteria.
fields.example: Review every active opportunity, reconcile incurred launch spending, and refresh the cash forecast. If two parcels remain promising but access documentation is pending, continue diligence without closing. If none qualifies, revise the selection thesis or pricing method. A documented rejection cohort is preferable to purchasing defective inventory to satisfy day-thirty optics.

fields.name: Weekly funnel and quality KPI definitions
fields.prompt: Define each funnel stage, denominator, reporting period, and evidence requirement. Include defect detection, source freshness, and turnaround measures so the pod can distinguish weak sourcing from slow execution or poor data quality.
fields.example: Report screened parcels, qualified parcels, owner responses, reviewed offers, accepted contracts, and completed sales as separate counts. If 20 of 100 screened parcels qualify, qualification is 20%; if four of twenty qualify for offers, offer readiness is 20%. Track unresolved access cases and median title-response days alongside conversion.

fields.name: Monthly earnings and capital KPI scorecard
fields.prompt: Record realized revenue, incurred expenses, owner profit, inventory cost, unrestricted cash, and aging by cohort. Connect results to the Base annual plan while avoiding straight-line revenue assumptions when closings are irregular or seasonal.
fields.example: One completed Base parcel contributes $85,000 revenue and $15,725 modeled owner profit after its $10,000 overhead allocation. Annual overhead still follows actual incurrence, so one closing does not prove monthly profitability. Track unsold parcels at ledger cost, cash separately, and progress toward ten completed sales without booking anticipated proceeds.

fields.name: Scale decision and score-component review
fields.prompt: Review the five score components against actual execution evidence. Identify the conditions required to increase inventory slots or staffing and show how the Scaled cost ceiling preserves the canonical owner-profit target.
fields.example: The 72 points comprise revenue potential 21, profit margin potential 18, team efficiency 17, startup accessibility 6, and automation potential 10. Scale only after repeatable closings, reliable access review, and adequate cash. At $1,500,000 proceeds, total costs must stay within $1,125,000 to preserve $375,000 owner profit and 25% margin.

fields.name: Parcel liquidation and business exit-readiness ledger
fields.prompt: List the records required for an individual parcel sale and a possible operating-business transfer. Separate inventory value from business earnings, identify nontransferable contracts, and document open claims, deposits, obligations, and owner-dependent activities.
fields.example: Each parcel file contains deed, title policy, survey evidence, tax status, cost ledger, market comparison, and active obligations. The business file adds reconciled earnings, provider contracts, data-license restrictions, and workflow documentation. Do not count inventory sale proceeds twice as both asset value and recurring earnings; obtain independent support for any proposed transfer valuation.

worksheets.completion_gate: By day thirty, the owner signs the launch review with actual activity counts, incurred spending, a refreshed cash forecast, assigned pod responsibilities, and an evidence-based next-month plan. Acquisition and scaling decisions remain tied to verified parcel quality, funded obligations, and canonical profit reconciliation rather than calendar pressure.
